country.comment: Rural villages in two states in India: Karnataka and Uttar Pradesh (Note 1 on PDF p. 22 notes Uttar Pradesh was subsequently divided into Uttar Pradesh and Uttaranchal, and the studied project spans both).
country.where_found: PDF p. 1, Title & Abstract; PDF pp. 5–6, Section III; PDF p. 22, Note 1

effect_estimate.comment: Note on PDF font encoding: in Tables 3–5, minus signs are rendered as '7' and '<' as '5' (verified arithmetically: e.g., in Table 4, 0.364 - (-0.676) = 1.04 and 0.497 - (-0.252) = 0.749). Both PSM treatment effects on household water outcomes (Tables 4–5) and bivariate probit determinants of participation (Tables 2–3) are reported.
effect_estimate.value: Propensity score matching (nearest-5-neighbours with replacement) shows both forms of household participation significantly improve the PCA water-improvements index and binary project satisfaction in the pooled sample: (1) Capital cost contribution increases water improvements by +1.04 index points (Treatment = 0.364 vs. Control = -0.676, t = 4.26) and satisfaction by +0.355 (0.813 vs. 0.458, t = 8.54); (2) Planning meeting attendance increases water improvements by +0.749 index points (0.497 vs. -0.252, t = 3.46) and satisfaction by +0.105 (0.790 vs. 0.685, t = 4.16). Disaggregated by region, meeting attendance significantly improves water index in UP Hills (+1.40, t = 2.51) and N. Karnataka (+0.330, t = 1.78, p < 0.10) and satisfaction in UP Hills (+0.309, t = 2.90), while capital cost contribution significantly increases satisfaction only in UP Hills (+0.561, t = 5.14) and has no statistically significant regional effect on water improvements. By wealth (Table 5), the poorest asset quartile gains significantly from meeting attendance in both water improvements (+1.680, t = 3.92) and satisfaction (+0.3717, t = 4.32), whereas the richest quartile sees no significant water-improvement gain from meeting attendance (-0.0331, t = -0.09) alongside higher satisfaction (+0.1984, t = 2.55); capital cost contribution yields water improvements for both lowest (+0.962, t = 1.93) and highest (+0.733, t = 1.99) quartiles. Descriptive rates: 41% of households attended a planning meeting (n = 1,508) and 59% contributed cash, labour, or materials toward the 10% capital cost share (n = 1,408). In weighted bivariate probit regressions (N = 1,158), SC/ST households (beta = -0.377, t = -2.69, p < 0.01), larger villages (beta = -0.00107, t = -6.53, p < 0.01), and higher village wealth disparity (beta = -0.138, t = -2.31, p < 0.05) were significantly less likely to contribute capital costs, whereas wealthier, more literate, and larger households were significantly more likely to participate.
effect_estimate.where_found: PDF p. 10, Table 2; PDF pp. 12–14, Table 3; PDF pp. 18–19, Section VII & Tables 4–5

mechanism_certainty.comment: Although PSM is appraised with ROBINS-I, overall risk of bias is Serious (excluding level 3) due to self-selection on unobservables (explicitly noted by the author on PDF p. 16 as a source of bias), retrospective post-implementation recall of pre-project water conditions, and within-village spillover across shared water schemes. Rated 1 because the study establishes statistical associations/matched differences using household survey data rather than directly observing committee decision-making or service allocation mechanisms.
mechanism_certainty.where_found: PDF pp. 6–8, Sections IV–V; PDF pp. 15–19, Section VII

mechanism_flags.comment: Both World Bank-assisted rural water projects mandated Village Water and Sanitation Committees, ~10% community capital cost contributions in cash/labour/materials (fees under BURDEN), and community planning meetings/Gram Sabhas/Community Action Plans (participation under DISCRETION_ACCOMMODATION), with NGO pre-planning capacity building and SARAR facilitation to include marginalized groups in Uttar Pradesh contrasted with Karnataka (bureaucratic_assistance).
mechanism_flags.where_found: PDF pp. 5–6, Section III; PDF p. 10, Section VI; PDF pp. 15–19, Section VII

outcome_flags.comment: The household water improvements PCA outcome index (PDF p. 16) explicitly combines seven household-level measures: perceived access to the source, change in distance to nearest source, and change in collection time (water_access); change in water source reliability (service_reliability); perceived adequacy of water from the new source (service_quantity, alongside perceived pressure change); and perceived change in water quality (service_quality). Household satisfaction is also analyzed (not a separate §5 code).
outcome_flags.where_found: PDF p. 16, Section VII; PDF pp. 18–19, Tables 4–5

publication_year.comment: Published in Journal of Development Studies, Vol. 45, No. 4, April 2009 (final version received November 2007).

risk_of_bias_tool.comment: To evaluate the impact of household participation ('treatment') on water improvements and satisfaction under self-selection, Section VII implements propensity score matching (PSM, nearest-5-neighbours with replacement on common support) comparing participating treatment households against matched non-participating control households; per RISK_OF_BIAS.md §1, non-randomized intervention evaluations using PSM map to ROBINS-I (alongside cross-sectional weighted bivariate probit regressions in Section VI for determinants of participation).
risk_of_bias_tool.where_found: PDF p. 1, Abstract; PDF pp. 15–19, Section VII & Tables 4–5

sample_size.comment: 45 villages randomly selected across two World Bank-assisted rural water projects (Karnataka and Uttar Pradesh), surveying ~40 households per village (or full census in villages with <40 households) in 1999–2000; PSM models further trim observations outside common support at the low end of propensity scores (exact trimmed PSM N not tabulated).
sample_size.value: 1,523 households surveyed across 45 villages (valid n = 1,508 households for planning meeting attendance; valid n = 1,408 households for capital cost contribution; full-sample bivariate probit N = 1,158 households, with regional subsamples N = 289 UP Hills, N = 340 S. Karnataka, N = 338 N. Karnataka)
sample_size.where_found: PDF pp. 6–7, Section IV; PDF p. 10, Table 2; PDF p. 14, Table 3; PDF p. 16, Section VII

study_design.comment: Combines cross-sectional weighted bivariate probit models of participation determinants (Section VI) with quasi-experimental propensity score matching (PSM) comparing self-selected participating ('treatment') vs. matched non-participating ('control') households on post-project water improvements and satisfaction (Section VII).
study_design.value: Cross-sectional household survey (random sample of villages and systematic/census sampling of households) analyzed with weighted bivariate probit regression for determinants of participation and propensity score matching (nearest-5-neighbours with replacement) for household-level participation impacts
study_design.where_found: PDF p. 1, Abstract; PDF pp. 6–8, Sections IV–V; PDF pp. 10–11, Section VI; PDF pp. 15–16, Section VII
